messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Posterior Predictive Distribution for Hieararchical Logistic Regressions
parts:
Dear Bob,

Thanks for your reply. I am interested in predictions for both: a new member for the existing group and the new whole group.

My model is below. The random effect of  the Year "a[year[N]])" includes 8 individual years.
For a new whole group, or new typical year, I was thinking to generate a random sample from Normal(mu_a, sigma_a) and then plug in my logistic equation (inverse logit (alpha+x * b).

For the individual group members or years,  I have eight a[1], a[2] ...a[8]  means and 8 standard deviations.Posterior means for  a[1], a[2] ...a[8] all include zero by the design. Which mean should I use for individual year predictions?

Am I on the right track? My Stan code is below. Thank you,

Peter

##################New model
model = "

data {
int<lower=0>K;
int<lower=0> N;
matrix[N,K]  x;
int<lower=0,upper=1> y[N];
int<lower=0> n_year; 
int<lower=1,upper=n_year> year[N];
}
parameters {
vector[n_year] a;
vector[K] b;
real<lower=0,upper=100> sigma_a;
real alpha;
real mu_a;
}
model { 
y ~ bernoulli_logit(alpha+x * b+a[year[N]]);
b ~ normal(0, 100);
 mu_a ~ normal(0, 10);
sigma_a~cauchy(0, 10);
  a ~ normal (mu_a, sigma_a);
}
"

messages.author: da33143a8db60ce8
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Posterior Predictive Distribution for Hieararchical Logistic Regressions
parts:
Hi—to get posterior predictive you’ll want to do this in generated quantities.  If you want a new group, you can define a_rep and y_rep and then, in generated quantities, generate a_rep first and then y_rep.  I’d also recommend stronger priors in your model, something more like N(0,1) or Cauchy(0,1) rather than scales of 10 or 100.  Just make sure your model is scaled appropriately (i.e, that x is of order 1 and that y is not an extremely rare event) and that should be fine.
A
